item.title: GT Voice: Wall Street's bet on China is about more than finance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 23:57:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Bloomberg recently published an article headlined "Wall Street Banks Are Finally Seeing Their China Bets Pay Off." As more Chinese companies take their businesses global, the likes of JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs are riding a wave of dealmaking. Some business lines are now posting double-digit revenue growth. But Wall Street's bets on China go beyond a pickup in dealmaking. They reflect a broader transformation in the Chinese economy. "In the next five years, a new wave of true multinational corporations will emerge from China," Alan Ho, JPMorgan's co-senior country officer for China, told Bloomberg. Their growth is opening up a fresh wave of business opportunities for foreign companies. China has kept investment bankers unusually busy this year. Bloomberg reported that some Morgan Stanley bankers pulled multiple all-nighters through the peak summer months. One even gave up a week-long vacation. These late nights at foreign investment banks in China offer a glimpse of the growing opportunities that the country's changing business landscape is creating for foreign firms. The story does not end with bankers. Foreign companies are finding new reasons to deepen their presence in China. Their role is no longer confined to financing Chinese companies or supporting their overseas expansion. Many are directly involved in China's economic transformation and global outreach, making them participants in this new wave of globalization. The trade figures offer a clearer picture. In the first half of 2026, trade by foreign-invested enterprises in China grew 17.1 percent year-on-year. These firms accounted for nearly 40 percent of China's exports to South Korea, close to 30 percent of exports to the EU and more than 30 percent of exports to emerging markets such as Mexico and Vietnam. Trade by foreign-invested firms in the electronic information sector grew 57.4 percent. China's new wave of globalization is opening up new ways for foreign companies to engage with its economy. They are not only supporting Chinese businesses as they expand overseas, but also taking a more direct part in China's economic development. In this sense, foreign companies are clear beneficiaries of China's latest economic developments. This helps explain why foreign companies are betting on China. As technological progress drives China's economic transformation, foreign companies are betting not only on its domestic consumer market, but also on opportunities in its industrial supply chains, technological advances and the global expansion of Chinese businesses. Some foreign firms are even moving from "in China, for China" to "in China, for the world," gaining access to a wider range of opportunities. As more Chinese companies go global, a new dynamic is emerging between China's economy and foreign businesses. The late-night lights at Morgan Stanley's offices are one small sign of this trend. Yet much of this is missing from the Western debate. As Chinese companies and products reach more overseas markets, some commentators see a threat, warning of a so-called "China shock 2.0." Such a zero-sum view looks increasingly detached from commercial realities. As more Chinese firms go global, some see a shock; others see new business. A number of foreign firms, however, are finding a fresh wave of opportunity in the international expansion of Chinese capital and companies. Bloomberg quoted Johannes Petry, a research director at Goethe University Frankfurt, who is working on a book about Wall Street in China, as saying: "The opportunity is increasingly tied to Chinese capital and companies going out into the world." Seizing these opportunities may be harder than it sounds. Competition in China is intense. But the growing number of foreign companies betting on China, and not just Wall Street banks, points to a broader trend. This is not simply a vote of confidence in China's economy; it is backed by real business growth. The late nights in some of those offices may be just the beginning.

item.title: A single TBM should not become a source of friction between China and India: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 23:44:00
Workers check up the performance of a tunnel boring machine (TBM) that begins its dig through a tunnel section in Beijing's Tongzhou district on December 28, 2023. This TBM, with a diameter of 13.3 meters and a length of 138 meters, is the largest one currently serving in Beijing and plans to use five months to complete a passage of 1,285 meters.Photo: VCG India's ambition to develop its domestic manufacturing industry and China's right to safeguard its national security are not inherently at odds. A single TBM should not become a source of friction between China and India. By setting aside excessive sensitivities and allowing technical issues to be addressed through appropriate technical channels, the two countries can create more room for the improvement of bilateral relations. China's export controls on tunnel boring machines (TBMs) have recently drawn considerable attention in India. India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal recently stated publicly that if China did not supply TBMs, India would develop them domestically, insisting that "India is not one to bow down." The remarks received coverage in Indian and some Western media, with many portraying the issue as a story of "India refusing to yield to China's 'chokehold'" and even interpreting it as a new flashpoint in China-India relations. Some narratives have become increasingly far-fetched, straying considerably from the facts. The origins of the controversy are straightforward. On October 19, China announced new export controls on critical machinery, including TBMs, various types of shield and rock tunnel boring machines, effective November 18. According to the relevant authorities, at least three points are clear. First, the items included in these measures have a clear dual-use nature and can be applied for both military and civilian purposes, and China's lawful implementation of export control measures conforms to international practices. Second, the announcement does not name any country, and the controls are not directed at any specific party. Third, the measures center on licensing rather than an outright export ban. Applications for compliant exports to legitimate civilian projects will be approved, provided the end users and end uses are clearly identified and meet the relevant requirements. India may have some misunderstandings or even complaints about these measures, and that is understandable. The country is in the midst of an intensive infrastructure-building drive. Whether for metro networks, high-speed rail projects, highways or water conservancy tunnels, India has considerable demand for large-scale excavation equipment such as TBMs. However, concerns over this issue should remain at the technical level. There is little need to politicize a routine export-control matter, let alone elevate it into a question of whether India will "never bow down" or defend its "national dignity." As for speculations that China is deliberately seeking to "restrict India's use of TBMs in border areas," they say more about the insecurity of those making them than about China's intentions. In fact, legitimate civilian projects have little reason for concern, and there are precedents for resolving similar issues. In 2024, India raised concerns over delays in customs clearance for TBMs manufactured in China by a German company. Minister Goyal also brought up the matter with visiting German officials. Following communication and coordination between China and India, the issues were resolved, and some of the equipment was subsequently delivered in a smooth manner. During Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's visit to India in 2025, China also assured the Indian side of addressing Indian key concerns relating to TBMs and other matters. This demonstrates that technical and regulatory issues of this kind can be resolved rationally through existing bilateral channels. A confrontational mindset will only narrow the space for pragmatic consultations, ultimately jeopardizing India's own infrastructure projects and development progress. India's ambition to develop its domestic manufacturing industry and China's right to safeguard its national security are not inherently at odds. India's pursuit of "self-reliance" and its active efforts to build domestic TBM manufacturing capabilities are legitimate aspirations for its own industrial upgrading. At the same time, China, as an exporter of controlled items, has an equally legitimate right to safeguard its national security and fulfill its international obligations. China has never viewed India's development as a threat to itself. As long as India provides Chinese companies with a fair and non-discriminatory business environment, the more advanced India's infrastructure and manufacturing sectors become, the greater the potential market demand and opportunities for cooperation between the two countries. In short, China is not that "petty." It's particularly crucial to remind India to remain vigilant against attempts by some Western voices to sow discord between the two countries. We have noticed that certain US media outlets have shown particular "enthusiasm" for the TBM issue. Bloomberg, for example, claimed that China's relevant export controls on TBMs are "a trade war risk to India," while The New York Times portrayed China's industrial strengths as a source of economic leverage and asserted that Beijing was building up its arsenal of economic weapons. Such reports deliberately disregard established international practices regarding export controls and omit the licensing application procedures and bilateral communication channels that China has kept open. In essence, these outlets would welcome mutual suspicion and confrontation between China and India, two major emerging powers, even at the cost of draining both countries' resources. They are not genuinely concerned about whether India's infrastructure projects can proceed smoothly. Their real objective is to drive a wedge between China and India. India should maintain an independent, clear-headed understanding and judgment of these narratives. Objectively speaking, reactions from various sectors in India also demonstrate how important pragmatic China-India cooperation is to India at this stage. The improvement in bilateral relations has not come easily, and both sides should devote more energy to expanding cooperation rather than allowing an export control issue involving a specific product to undermine the broader relationship. A single TBM should not become a source of friction between China and India. By setting aside excessive sensitivities and allowing technical issues to be addressed through appropriate technical channels, the two countries can create more room for the improvement of bilateral relations.

item.title: Annual CIIE opens in Shanghai, showcasing China's commitment to opening up
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 23:37:00
Visitors watch a robot tea ceremony performance in the China Pavilion at the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai on November 5, 2026. Photo: Xinhua On Thursday morning, in the waiting lounge of the opening ceremony of the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, two hours before the ceremony began, the guests had already begun arriving. They took selfies, chatted, posed for group photos with old friends and gave interviews to the media. According to on-site observations by the Global Times, in the relaxing atmosphere, the words they mentioned most were "opportunity", "openness" and "market." Running from Thursday to Tuesday next week, this year's CIIE has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors, with total exhibition area exceeding 440,000 square meters. Over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debut at the event, the highest number in history. In addition, nearly 200 companies and institutions have been "full attendees" at the CIIE for all nine editions. In his keynote speech at the opening ceremony, Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that the CIIE has witnessed China's firm determination and concrete actions to promote high-standard opening-up, the remarkable results and tremendous gains of businesses and people from various countries in sharing opportunities in the Chinese market, and the unremitting efforts and important contributions of visionary people from all walks of life in improving global economic governance, according to Xinhua News Agency. This fully demonstrates China's strategic resolve in advancing high-standard opening-up, injecting valuable certainty, stability and confidence in development into the world, Hu Qimu, professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Thursday. Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker of Austria, and UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo attended the opening ceremony and delivered remarks, Xinhua reported. Big welcome Ding's speech was welcomed by many executives from global multinational companies, who said they draw great inspiration from the speech and remain confident in honoring their long-term commitment to China. Rogier Janssens, President of Merck China, told the Global Times that CIIE brings the world to China, and gives China a stronger voice in the global conversation. "As China moves into its 15th Five-Year Plan, the Expo's role is even more important," Janssens said. The CIIE opening ceremony underscored the importance of openness, collaboration and innovation-driven development, further reinforcing Henkel's confidence in the long-term growth of the Chinese market, Anna An, President of Henkel China told the Global Times on Thursday. Vice Premier Ding's speech reaffirmed China's steadfast commitment to high-standard opening-up and highlighted the country's important role in driving growth and building an open global economy, echoed Poh-Yian Koh, President of FedEx China. These remarks were made as exhibitors from around the world flocked to the event in droves. Official data showed that US exhibitors occupy more than 50,000 square meters, leading for the eighth consecutive year, while companies from Germany, the UK and France also rank among the top participants. Jim Sutter, CEO of the US Soybean Export Council, was among the first batch of representatives of American soybean exporters. "We've been doing work in China since 1982, so 44 years' history here. And I think the CIIE has become such a big event, and it's just something you can't miss. If you're doing business in China, you need to be at the CIIE," Sutter told the Global Times. "It's extremely important for the US to continue to sell soybean into China, "Andrew Moore, director of the American Soybean Association (ASA), told the Global Times. This year, the ASA has brought their biggest exhibition area ever in the event, according to Moore. Valuing the Chinese market and embracing new cooperation opportunities is a shared sentiment among many of the representatives present. "China is a very, very good market for Moldova products. Moldova is a big wine producer… and we hope to have a bigger market in China," said Claudiu Nasui, Minister of Economic Development and Digitalization of Moldova. "China accounts for 30 percent of Shiseido's global market share, and is one of the most important markets for us. With 45 years' presence in China, we are continuing to bring new innovations here. We deeply understand Chinese consumers and will identify opportunities to create together with local Chinese consumers," said Toshinobu Umetsu, CEO of Shiseido China and Travel Retail Region. Big market A report released by Beijing Normal University and the China Association for International Trade on Wednesday said China's position as an important export destination for countries around the world is becoming increasingly prominent. From 2001 to 2025, the share of global exports to China in total global exports showed an overall steady upward trend, the report said. China is not only the main destination of exports, it is also a big market for global players. China has remained the world's second-largest import market for 17 consecutive years, with its total imports exceeding 90 trillion yuan during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), and the pace is picking up. China's imports reached 16.7 trillion yuan in the first nine months of 2026, up 22.3 percent, the fastest growth since 2021, according to the Xinhua News Agency. China's increasingly sophisticated consumer demand is creating new opportunities for global businesses beyond its massive market size. From healthier diets and beauty products to outdoor sports and leisure experiences, the country's growing middle-income population is driving demand for a broader range of goods and services, even for new friends. On Thursday afternoon, Pierre Fabre Group made its debut showing at the CIIE. Eric Ducournau, CEO of the group, said that the innovation vitality and development potential demonstrated by the Chinese market have strengthened its confidence in deeply cultivating the Chinese market over the long term. For multinational companies, putting roots down in China is not just about sharing in market dividends — it is about deeply integrating with China's ecosystem and expanding the incremental pie of innovation and consumption, said Hu. Looking ahead to the vast prospects of social consumption and the service sector under the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), China will remain a major historic opportunity shared by the world, Hu added. "CIIE is important for learning about what the Chinese market needs and also to identify what are the things that developing countries can do to access the Chinese market. My expectation for next year is that more countries can participate in the Chinese market," Luz Ma de la Mora, director of UNCTAD's Division on International Trade and Commodities, told the Global Times on Thursday. "Chinese companies can also help developing countries to integrate into their supply chains, not only for Chinese market, but also for the global markets," Mora said.

item.title: China's Ministry of Water Resources to plan flood and drought prevention in advance in response to the strongest El Nino event on record
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 23:18:00
Vehicles travel through a flooded road in Longwan district, Wenzhou, East China's Zhejiang Province, on August 28. Photo: Screenshot from Xinhua News Agency China's Ministry of Water Resources said on Thursday that it would begin planning flood and drought prevention efforts for 2027 ahead of time, building on its regular prevention and response measures, amid the continued development of the strongest El Nino event on record and the delayed effects of the exceptionally strong climate phenomenon, thepaper.cn reported. China's National Climate Center confirmed that an exceptionally strong El Nino event emerged in the equatorial central and eastern Pacific in September 2026, developed into the strongest El Nino event on record in October, and is expected to peak in late autumn or early winter. Compared with the three previous exceptionally strong El Nino events on record, the current event stands out for its rapid development and potentially record-breaking intensity. It took just five months to reach exceptionally strong levels, and its peak could exceed 3.2 C. Forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization's Global Producing Centres indicate an "exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100 percent" that the El Nino will persist through to February 2027. During a press briefing on Thursday, Yao Wenguang, director general of the department of flood and drought disaster prevention of the Ministry of Water Resources, highlighted the delayed effects of El Nino and their potential impact on China. The likelihood of extreme weather and climate events is expected to increase in 2027, Yao said, warning that the extreme and destructive nature of flood disasters, as well as their compound and cascading effects, could become more pronounced, placing higher demands on flood prevention and defense systems, infrastructure resilience, and operational coordination and command. The ministry will take a systematic approach to flood prevention, repairing flood-damaged infrastructure, strengthening flood-control systems and accelerating the deployment and networking of rainfall-monitoring radars in high-risk areas and key river basins. Meanwhile, the ministry will strengthen proactive risk management by closely tracking the exceptionally strong El Nino and continuously assessing its potential impacts on China's rainfall, temperatures and flood and drought risks. It will thoroughly identify and address potential risks in areas at risk of extreme rainstorms, river basin floods, flash floods, droughts and rapid shifts between drought and flooding, and take preventive measures well in advance. Besides, the ministry will accelerate the digitalization and intelligent upgrading of water management, improving integrated monitoring systems, high-fidelity digital models and flood-management applications. It will also promote the development and deployment of new technologies and equipment, and upgrade China's digital twin system for water management to strengthen flood and drought disaster response capabilities. China experienced pronounced climate anomalies in 2026, with concentrated typhoon landfalls, frequent intense rainfall, simultaneous river flooding and severe localized droughts, thepaper.cn reported. A total of 31 typhoons formed over the western North Pacific and the South China Sea this year, seven of which made landfall in China. Both figures were higher than their respective long-term averages, according to thepaper.cn. Global Times

item.title: China's ocean governance efforts win international recognition as Xiamen hosts World Ocean Week
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 22:47:00
Participants take selfies in front of China's Jiaolong manned submersible during the 2026 World Ocean Week in Xiamen, East China's Fujian Province, on November 5, 2026. Photo: Courtesy of the organizers of the 2026 World Ocean Week in Xiamen Xiamen, a coastal city in East China's Fujian Province, brought together government officials, representatives of international organizations and marine experts from around the world on Thursday as the 2026 World Ocean Week opened, with discussions focusing on ocean conservation and sustainable development. As the Agreement on Marine Biodiversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement) entered into force this year, global ocean governance has moved into a new phase of implementation. China has been actively involved in advancing international marine conservation, including bidding to host the BBNJ Secretariat, promoting the establishment of marine protected areas in Antarctica, and cooperating with island countries on issues such as climate change. International guests at the event praised China's contributions. José María Figueres, former president of Costa Rica, told the Global Times on Thursday that he welcomed China's efforts, citing its role in global biodiversity initiatives and its proposal for a marine protected area in the Cosmonauts Sea near East Antarctica. Figueres noted China's contribution to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), which sets a global target of effectively conserving and managing at least 30 percent of terrestrial and inland water areas, as well as coastal and marine areas, by 2030. He also praised China's proposal for marine protection in Antarctica, describing the region as one of the world's most pristine and delicate environments. These efforts, alongside China's recent steps to strengthen environmental protection at home, demonstrate its engagement with international efforts to protect the ocean and biodiversity, he said. In Figueres' view, they also position China well to host the BBNJ Secretariat. Manal Khaled Sayed Ahmed, an Egyptian participant at the event, also welcomed the international cooperation on display at the event. She said she was pleased to see people of different nationalities coming together around the shared goal of protecting the ocean and safeguarding marine resources for future generations. China has played a significant role in demonstrating how the ocean and its resources can contribute to future development and investment, Ahmed said. She added that China had set an example by encouraging countries to make effective use of their own resources. Alongside the international discussion, Xiamen's own approach to marine conservation and sustainable development has also attracted attention. Grethel Aguilar, director general of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), described Xiamen as a particularly appropriate place for discussions on ocean issues, noting its vibrant blue economy and the close connection between the sea and the city's development, economy, food systems and residents' well-being. Xiamen and Fujian have a long record of working with the sea rather than against it, Aguilar said, pointing to coastal wetland and mangrove restoration, as well as advances in marine science at the Fujian Ocean Innovation Center. She described this combination of practical action and science-based approaches as the kind of work needed to address global ocean challenges. The opening ceremony also saw the launch of the "Xinghai-BBNJ" ecological data service, developed by a national key laboratory for satellite-based marine monitoring. It integrates six datasets covering sea surface temperatures, global ocean temperature and salinity, Lagrangian eddies, nitrate, chlorophyll and dissolved oxygen, alongside the Mazu ecological coupling model. The seven products can help establish ocean environmental baselines, track ecosystem changes and simulate future scenarios, supporting scientific assessments and long-term monitoring of marine protected areas on the high seas. Turning international commitments into effective protection, however, requires more than agreements and institutional arrangements. It also calls for stronger scientific understanding and closer coordination between research and policymaking. Dai Minhan, a chair professor of marine environmental science at Xiamen University and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said the implementation of the BBNJ Agreement faces challenges including gaps in scientific knowledge, uneven access to marine data and fragmentation in existing governance systems. Large areas of the ocean remain poorly understood, while available data are unevenly distributed across regions, Dai noted. At the same time, marine ecosystems are constantly changing under pressures such as acidification and pollution. These dynamics make it difficult for policymakers to rely on static information or respond only after environmental damage has occurred. Dai called for a shift beyond simply supplying scientific information toward developing what he described as "policy-level science" - a closer, ongoing interaction between scientific research and policymaking. Under this approach, scientific evidence, policy discussions and feedback would form a continuous process, allowing decisions to adapt as knowledge and environmental conditions evolve. He also emphasized the importance of international cooperation built around joint design, involving countries in defining research priorities, coordinating ocean observations, sharing data and models, and strengthening the scientific and technical capacities of developing countries. Xiamen University has established a support system integrating scientific research, observation, technological innovation and international cooperation since 1983, Dai said. Its research platforms and international networks could help connect scientific knowledge with practical governance needs and contribute to international cooperation. The challenge now is to ensure that global commitments translate into measurable improvements in ocean health. As the BBNJ Agreement enters its implementation phase, Xiamen's experience offers a local perspective on how marine conservation, scientific research and international partnerships can reinforce one another. The task of protecting the ocean goes far beyond the efforts of any single country or city. Turning shared commitments into effective action will depend on sustained cooperation, accessible scientific knowledge and the collective ability to respond to challenges that cross national boundaries, experts noted.

item.title: EU's reported China deterrence plans risk hurting competitiveness, raising costs for EU manufacturers and undermining bilateral cooperation: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 22:36:00
The European Union (EU) flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG The European Commission (EC) on Wednesday unveiled its 2027 work program, outlining plans for a dedicated diversification instrument, which the bloc claimed was intended to strengthen its resilience and accelerate supply chain diversification, as Brussels reportedly continues to consider further restrictions on Chinese imports. The EU's push to reduce so-called overreliance on China through trade restrictions could backfire by raising costs for European manufacturers and weakening their competitiveness, while undermining China-EU economic cooperation and mutual trust, Chinese experts warned. In the work program, the EC explicitly referred to the Chinese market, asserting that access to it, along with "cheap" imported energy and raw materials and open global trade, was no longer the foundation for a thriving EU economy that it once was. The bloc claimed that economic independence had therefore become a priority for Europe. Euronews reported on October 29 that the diversification proposal was directly aimed at Beijing, linking it to concerns over the bloc's reliance on Chinese supplies of critical raw materials and other strategic products. Notably, the diversification plan has raised concerns among European businesses about the costs of finding alternative suppliers. "Companies are already doing the maximum to have a cost-effective structure," Luisa Santos, deputy director-general at BusinessEurope, told Euronews. "If they are working with certain suppliers, it is because they are the ones that have the best offer in terms of the product, regarding its cost and performance." "There is nothing inherently wrong with diversifying supply chains, as this is a choice the EU is free to make. However, diversification should not be driven by the politically motivated goal of decoupling from China or imposing artificial barriers on normal trade," Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Thursday. If diversification policies are primarily aimed at arbitrarily decoupling from China, they could undermine the stable and mutually beneficial economic and trade ties between China and the EU, Jian said. The proposals come as Brussels continues to imposes restrictions on trade with China, prompting firm responses form the Chinese side. On Thursday, Huang Ling, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce, criticized the EU's introduction of a 2-euro handling fee on low-value imports starting November 1, following the implementation of a 3-euro tariff in July, and the combined impact of the two measures on Chinese cross-border e-commerce exporters. Huang said China is paying close attention to the EU's new regulations, noting that cross-border e-commerce, as a new form and model of international trade, provides businesses and consumers around the world with a diverse range of choices. Many Chinese products imported by Europe are intermediate goods used in manufacturing. Replacing them with supplies from other sources could significantly increase production costs and weaken European companies' competitiveness, while reduced access to affordable consumer goods could add to inflationary pressures, Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Thursday. Moreover, the unilateral restrictions could undermine respect for World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and erode trust in China-EU trade talks, said Hu. China has repeatedly emphasized the importance of addressing economic and trade differences through dialogue. "China is not the root cause of the EU's problems, but a partner in addressing them... Rather than resorting to further trade restrictions, the EU should adopt a more pragmatic approach, strengthen dialogue with China, and pursue mutually beneficial cooperation to address economic challenges and enhance industrial competitiveness," said Hu.

item.title: How China's accessible cloud tech and AI are revolutionizing crop monitoring worldwide to build food security in developing countries
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 21:52:00
A CropWatch team member trains Ethiopian agricultural technicians on field measurement data collection standards in Ethiopia in April 2026. Photo: Courtesy of Wu Bingfang Editor's Note: As global challenges grow increasingly interconnected, technological solutions are rarely confined to a single country. Through research collaboration, open sharing of expertise and partnerships with international institutions, Chinese scientists, engineers and enterprises are engaging more deeply with the world, contributing tools and experience to problems that demand collective answers. The Global Times launches the "Tech Seeds, Global Bloom" series, spotlighting China's achievements in advancing tech for good both domestically and internationally. By following these trajectories, the series invites readers to consider a different measure of progress: Not how advanced technology becomes, but whom it ultimately serves, and how widely its benefits can spread. This is the ninth installment. China's CropWatch system is helping developing countries build their own crop-monitoring capabilities, supporting more timely and informed food security decisions. The technology is being adapted to local needs, while international cooperation is also driving new research and bringing advanced remote sensing tools within reach of more users. Zhang Miao, an associate professor at the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS), opens the crop-monitoring interface of CropWatch, a remote sensing-based global crop monitoring cloud platform, on his computer. With a few clicks, a graph showing the growth of rice in a central province of Cambodia appears on the screen. Soil moisture, rainfall anomalies and vegetation indices unfold along a timeline, offering a detailed picture of how crops have developed over time. Earth observation and crop monitoring on a massive scale are neither easy nor inexpensive exercises, but both hold immense potential for better food security planning and progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. Yet, many developing countries simply do not have access to the required tools, either due to technology deficits or costs, said the UN Trade and Development. CropWatch is helping to bridge that gap. Developed by AIRCAS, formerly known as IRSA, in 1998, the system combines satellite remote sensing with ground-based observations to independently assess crop area, crop growth, yield and production, as well as agricultural disaster at national and global scales. Originally designed for domestic use, its application has since been extended to countries and regions around the world. Moreover, the system has continued to evolve as new remote sensing data emerge, monitoring methods improve and artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into the system. On October 16, AIRCAS received the 2026 Achievement Award from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) for its development of CropWatch. Wu Bingfang, a professor at the AIRCAS who leads the CropWatch team, traveled to Rome to accept the award. "Turning a complex crop-monitoring process into one that anyone can use represents a major technological advance," Wu told the Global Times. "It is also highly consistent with China's Global Development Initiative, which identifies food security as a key area of cooperation." "Our goal has always been to put crop-monitoring capabilities directly into the hands of more countries, so they can see for themselves what is happening in their own breadbaskets," he said. Wu Bingfang, a professor at the AIRCAS who leads the CropWatch team, trains staff from the Office of Agricultural Economics under Thailand's Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives on rice area monitoring technology in Thailand in February 2025. Photo: Courtesy of Zhang Miao From receiving information to producing it In 2015, Wu made his first visit to Mozambique. During a visit to the World Bank's country office, he came across a booklet outlining the country's food security situation. What he read brought home the practical consequences of a country lacking the ability to monitor its own agricultural production. "The challenge was immense," Wu recalled. "Mozambique stretches long and narrow from north to south, with weak transport and communications infrastructure. As a result, the central government struggles to keep timely track of crop conditions across the country, especially in remote areas. When harvests fail, relief cannot arrive in time; when harvests are good, agricultural produce cannot be shipped out in time. The lack of timely crop information compounds these constraints." The experience reminded him of the challenges the team had faced when developing China's own crop monitoring capabilities. At that time, the country lacked an independent operational system and relied heavily on monitoring reports from other countries with established systems to understand agricultural conditions. "Having experienced that ourselves, and understanding the realities these countries face, I felt our crop-monitoring technology could be extremely useful to Mozambique and other countries in similar circumstances," Wu said. "That was why we decided to share it." Wu introduced that CropWatch's core technologies operate on two levels: innovative monitoring methods and an integrated operational system. Its unique methods include six proprietary indicators such as CROp Production Index (CroPI) and a crop-area estimation technique particularly designed for smallholder farming and complex agricultural landscapes, with an accuracy of around 97 percent. Meanwhile, its automated system can process global agricultural data in a single day with a core team of just six researchers and several students, making it highly efficient and well suited for deployment in developing countries. In 2017, with support from international organizations, the CropWatch cloud platform was made available to Mozambique, followed by a training program. Over the following three years, Mozambican technicians learned to operate the system independently, analyze crop conditions and incorporate their findings into national agro-meteorological bulletins in Portuguese. Previously, they had largely relied on scattered information gathered from the internet. Now, the analytical capability was increasingly in their own hands. The platform was customized to reflect differences in cropping patterns and monitoring priorities across Mozambique. It offered tailored indicators and functions covering agro-climatic and agronomic conditions, as well as early warning, allowing users to quantitatively assess weather conditions, crop growth and production prospects across cultivated areas. Training extended beyond software operation to include knowledge and skills in remote sensing for agriculture and field-based observation. Officials and technical personnel from Mozambique's Ministry of Agriculture, Environment and Fisheries, as well as provincial agricultural departments, received training courses. Users could select their own indicators and conduct online monitoring and analysis for specific areas, laying the groundwork for independent assessments at different administrative levels. The results were tangible. Since June 2018, Mozambique's Ministry of Agriculture, Environment and Fisheries had independently issued more than 20 crop-monitoring and food security early warning reports using the platform by 2022, according to its website. Mozambique was only the beginning. By October, CropWatch-related capacity-building activities had reached more than 40 countries, including Cambodia, Ethiopia, Laos, Mongolia, Nigeria, Mauritius, Thailand, Vietnam and Myanmar. More than 600 technical personnel had received training, and the system had been locally deployed in seven countries. Zhang Miao, an associate professor at the AIRCAS, trains Southern African trainees on using the CropWatch cloud platform at the University of Zambia in June 2026. Photo: Courtesy of Zhang Miao Local deployment, global innovation Making CropWatch work in different countries has not always been straightforward. Agricultural landscapes, crop varieties, farming practices and local environmental conditions can differ significantly from those in China. Wu said the answer lies in making users active participants in the development process. "CropWatch is an open system. If our partners have a good method, they can incorporate it into the platform and make use of the infrastructure we have built," he said. In Mongolia, the Chinese team and local partners jointly conducted in-situ measurements over five years to improve drought-monitoring models. After calibration, Mongolian technicians were trained to develop their own national monitoring approaches and incorporate them into the platform. As the platform evolves, AI is beginning to shorten the path from raw data to usable analysis. Zhang, who has participated in deployment and training projects in roughly two-thirds of the countries involved, told the Global Times that the team has integrated large language models into CropWatch, allowing users to generate draft analytical reports with a single command after country-specific monitoring products have been produced. But automation does not eliminate the need for human expertise. AI-generated reports still require professional review, and users must learn how to refine the results rather than submit them directly to decision-makers, Zhang said. For Zhang, however, the most important outcome of international training is not simply that partner countries learn to use an existing technology. It is that the experience exposes weaknesses in existing models and creates new directions for research. Zhang recalled the team's first visit to farmland in Mozambique. The plots were so overgrown that he initially struggled to recognize them as cultivated fields. In some areas, grass was as abundant as, or even more abundant than, the crops themselves. That creates a major challenge for satellite-based monitoring. The signals recorded by remote sensing instruments may come from weeds rather than the crops being monitored. If a model interprets dense vegetation as healthy crop growth, it could overestimate yields. Separating the signals of weeds from those of cultivated crops has therefore become an important research problem for the team led by Wu. The result therefore is a two-way process, Zhang said. "Chinese researchers help other countries build their monitoring capabilities, while local experience helps advance the underlying science." A global public good For Wu, the significance of CropWatch ultimately extends beyond remote sensing. "By making crop information more transparent, we hope to contribute to better global food security governance," he said. That ambition aligns with the Global Development Initiative, which identifies food security as one of its eight priority areas for international cooperation. Thanks to its own efforts, China, once a recipient of FAO technology, has turned to a core contributor to the organization. China has carried out agricultural cooperation with more than 140 countries and regions, provided more than 1,000 agricultural technologies to other developing countries and trained over 14,000 technicians on hybrid rice technology, China's Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian said on October 16, 2025. CropWatch is part of a broader effort to make Chinese agricultural science and technology more accessible internationally. Other examples include the MAZU agricultural application, which provides tailored frost forecasts for apple cultivation in Uzbekistan and services for wheat production and drought prevention in Tajikistan. Released to international users in 2025, the system has begun extending its services into Central Asia. The next stage of CropWatch development is already taking shape and could make this approach more accessible. Wu said his team has been developing a redesigned architecture built around open foundation data and an application programming interface (API) library. Beta versions are already being tested in countries such as Cambodia, Nigeria and Thailand, with promising results. As the new framework is further rolled out, users ranging from national agencies to individual farmers will be able to build their own monitoring systems using the underlying data and tools. With the development of AI agents, he envisions a future in which a farmer could simply ask a question on a smartphone - "What will my production be this year?" - and receive an accurate answer immediately. "Making remote sensing accessible to everyone, rather than leaving it as something confined to an ivory tower, is what I have pursued throughout my career," Wu said.

item.title: One year on, Fujian carrier pushes toward full combat capability
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 21:12:00
The commissioning and flag-presenting ceremony of the Fujian, China's first aircraft carrier equipped with electromagnetic catapults, is held at a naval port in Sanya City, South China's Hainan Province, on November 5, 2025. Photo: Xinhua November 5 marks the first anniversary of the commissioning of China's third aircraft carrier Fujian . Officially inducted on November 5, 2025, the Fujian is the first catapult-equipped carrier fully designed and built by China, and the world's first conventionally powered carrier with electromagnetic catapults. In its first year, the Fujian sailed south through the Taiwan Straits to the South China Sea, then north to the East China Sea and Yellow Sea, completing cross-theater trials and training, showing it can operate across sea zones in the far seas, with coordination with escorting vessels reaching a certain level, CCTV News reported on Thursday. CCTV reported that 2026 has been a critical year for the Fujian 's transition from initial combat capability to full combat capability. Military affairs experts told the Global Times that the Fujian has completed its leap from platform validation to system integration in its first year, and is pushing toward "full combat capability" through high-intensity training, propelling the PLA Navy into an era of three-carrier rotation. Initial combat capability Before the Fujian entered service, its activities were already being closely watched. On June 17, 2022, China's third aircraft carrier was launched and named the Fujian , with hull number 18. On May 1, 2024, the Fujian completed its first eight-day sea trial, testing propulsion, electrical and other systems, meeting expected targets. On September 22, 2025, the J-15T heavy fighter jet, the J-35 stealth fighter jet, and the KJ-600 early warning aircraft - all displayed at the 2025 V-Day parade - completed their first catapult takeoffs and landings aboard the Fujian , reported CCTV. After being officially commissioned, within half a month, it formed a carrier group with multiple vessels for its first live maritime training, with multiple carrier-based aircraft completing numerous catapult takeoffs and landings, validating the Fujian's electromagnetic catapult, recovery and deck operations, CCTV reported. Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Thursday that the Fujian now has cross-theater far-sea operational capability, with coordination with escorting vessels reaching a certain level, meaning it has basically formed combat capability. "Basically formed combat capability" means the Fujian can sail normally; its aircraft can take off and land on deck, and it can conduct basic formation training with escort vessels. "Full combat capability" requires a leap from "can sail, can take off and land, can fight limited battles" to "can conduct high-intensity, all-weather, system-based, sustained operations." At the same time, all ships in the group must coordinate closely to ensure the carrier strike group can sustain system-based operations in the far seas, Zhang said. The Fujian is now tackling these requirements one by one through high-intensity training. Zhang said three points of interest should be observed: first, full-deck, full-load sortie generation, upgrading from "can use catapult" to "can use catapult continuously at high intensity"; second, takeoffs and landings under complex conditions. Nighttime and severe sea states are recognized difficulties, and pilots must obtain night qualifications; third, deep integration of the formation system, achieving integrated command and information sharing between ships and aircraft. Far-sea training Far-sea training is the final piece of the puzzle for full combat capability, Song Zhongping, another Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Thursday. Since October 14, the PLA Navy's Liaoning carrier group has been training in relevant waters of the Western Pacific, a routine mission under the annual plan, aimed at testing and improving combat-oriented training and continuously enhancing mission capability. It complies with international law and practice and does not target any specific country or target, according to China's Ministry of Defense. Against this backdrop, Song said that given the past year's progress, the Fujian may soon be able to conduct similar far-sea training. Song explained that the Fujian has grown in three ways over its first year. First, after prolonged trial service, its hull lines, internal structure, electrical and propulsion systems and electromagnetic catapult support systems have all been effectively tested. "This is China's first large carrier with a flat deck. The Fujian 's first year shows its design is sound and meets China's actual needs for developing large carriers." Second, ship-aircraft coordination has produced substantive results. The Fujian has initial aviation combat, support and sustained operation capabilities. Third, it has begun building out the carrier strike group system. Over the past year, the Fujian has conducted multiple compatibility drills with escort vessels, practicing formation navigation, command coordination and joint ship-aircraft support. "This step is laying the foundation for a complete carrier strike group," Song said. Within a year, the Fujian jumped from "multiple carrier aircraft catapult takeoffs and landings, initial full-deck capability" to "live formation training, cross-theater maneuvers", with escort coordination reaching a certain level and initial combat capability achieved. "This pace is rare in the history of global carrier development, completing in one year what other countries took years to do." Song said the next step may see the Fujian carrier strike group head into the Western Pacific, or even more unfamiliar and complex waters, for far-sea deployments and combat-oriented trials, testing sustained operations, logistics support and adaptability to complex sea conditions. Value of three carriers With the Liaoning , Shandong and Fujian , the PLA Navy has entered the three-carrier era. "The real value of the three-carrier era is not the visual impact of three ships in one frame, but the system of rotation among 'on duty - training - maintenance'," Zhang stressed. Three carriers form the minimum threshold for sustained maritime presence: one on duty, one in training, and one in maintenance. Once rotation runs smoothly, carriers upgrade from scarce resources "pulled out when needed" to strategic tools "ready at any time." It's also possible the Fujian will conduct dual- or even triple-carrier group exercises with the Liaoning and Shandong , Song said. Such drills would be significant: they would show that China can mobilize multiple large carriers simultaneously, and dual- or triple-carrier drills with other services would be more targeted and closer to real combat. This means the Fujian strike group's deployment will gradually shift from "validating performance" to "fulfilling missions", and from "training the platform" to "training for the mission", Song said.

item.title: US think tank hypes 'China threat' in flawed bid to prop up fading hegemony
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 20:42:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT The Hudson Institute, a US think tank, recently released a report titled "Righting the ship: Building a relevant US navy fleet for twenty-first-century deterrence and combat." The report mentions "China" more than 60 times, portraying Beijing's maritime power as a "threat" and viewing it as the core competitive variable challenging US maritime hegemony. Taking a cross-Taiwan-Straits conflict as a preset scenario, it puts forward the so-called "hellscape" concept. Rather than a strategic analysis, this report reads more like a self-diagnosis of US anxiety over maritime supremacy: It accurately identifies the symptoms, yet prescribes the wrong remedy. The report acknowledges that US naval dominance, which has lasted for more than 80 years, is waning. Yet it begs a critical question: Is this erosion caused by China "challenging" US hegemony, or by home-grown woes such as the hollowed-out domestic shipbuilding industry, an aging fleet, and endless wars overseas? The report did not offer any valid answers to this question. The US shipbuilding industry is plagued by deep-seated problems, and the traditional approach of building large warships is no longer sustainable. Consequently, some in Washington have cited China's "System Destruction Warfare" as an external driver for reforming the US Navy. They advocate the large-scale deployment of unmanned maritime combat systems to build a counterforce capable of securing an advantage in maritime confrontations, while repeatedly wargaming ways to "deter and contain adversaries." What makes this line of thinking most dangerous lies not in its concrete military wargaming, but in its conceptual framework: It designates China as a hypothetical adversary, treats the Taiwan Straits as a potential battlefield, and simplistically interprets all maritime force-building as great-power rivalry. Such confrontational wargaming is more than a mere technical military assessment. Rooted in America's full set of security and political logic, it lays bare Washington's doctrine of absolute security. This mindset has remained consistent throughout US history. From its early days as a rising regional power to its pursuit of global hegemony, the US cannot tolerate the emergence of any nation capable of matching its power. Coupled with the outsized influence of the military-industrial complex on US policymaking and fiscal resource allocation after World War II, US defense policy has developed an ingrained logic, that is to imagine and hype up external threats in order to secure sustained government budget allocations for the military. This hegemonic mindset also highlights a defining characteristic of the US defense economy. Competition among the various branches of the US military over the annual defense budget is fierce, and the Navy, too, hopes to secure more funding for its branch by hyping "China threat" claims. This zero-sum mindset overlooks the fact that China is the world's largest trading nation, and the security of maritime shipping lanes is equally vital to China. The development of Chinese navy is not intended to challenge anyone, but rather to safeguard its legitimate maritime rights and interests and the security of its sea lanes. The development of China's Coast Guard forces corresponds to China's 32,000-kilometer coastline and extensive maritime economic interests; this is not expansion, but rather a necessary alignment. This also exposes the US Navy's misguided positioning in the Asia-Pacific. Rather than committing to serving as a contributor to regional security, it is eager to stoke tensions, playing the role of a disruptor in the region. The Asia-Pacific should be moving toward peace, prosperity, and stability, but the US deliberately stirs up confrontation and hypes the prospect of war to force regional countries into security dependence on the US and maintain unequal regional relations - a course of action that does not align with the aspirations of most countries in the Asia-Pacific. While verbally acknowledging that the US "can no longer recreate its past unchallenged dominance over the oceans," the report refuses to abandon its mindset of maritime hegemony. Its goal is not to adapt to a multipolar world, but to adopt a new set of tools to keep acting as the "world's policeman." From the "global deployment of aircraft carriers" to the "island-chain blockades using unmanned systems," only the tools have changed. What remains unchanged is the hegemonic obsession that Washington gets to call all the shots. This report by the Hudson Institute is a "plan to prop up fading hegemony." While it acknowledges the decline of US maritime power, it attributes the cause to "China's rise" rather than reflecting on America's own strategic overextension and industrial hollowing-out. It proposes technical solutions such as the "hellscape" strategy, yet sidesteps the most fundamental question: What right does the US have to deploy military forces on other countries' doorsteps? Rather than spending time devising "hellscape," US think tanks would do better to devote their energy to figuring out how to coexist peacefully with other major countries. After all, in the 21st-century world, hegemony is not the answer - coexistence is.

item.title: Harnessing desert sun: Chinese firms help advance UAE's clean energy transition
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 12:31:00
This undated drone photo shows a view of the 1.5-gigawatt Abu Dhabi PV3 Al Ajban solar project in northeastern Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates. With a Chinese company involved in its construction, the project is nearing grid connection, highlighting the growing China-UAE partnership in advancing the transition to low-carbon energy. (Power Construction Corporation of China/Handout via Xinhua) Under the bright desert sun, rows of photovoltaic panels stretch toward the horizon, their steel mounts casting parallel shadows on pale-yellow sand. The vast solar array is part of the 1.5-gigawatt Abu Dhabi PV3 Al Ajban solar project in northeastern Abu Dhabi. With a Chinese company involved in its construction, the project is nearing grid connection, highlighting the growing China-UAE partnership in advancing the transition to low-carbon energy. Inside the substation area, electrical equipment of different sizes stands in orderly rows, while workers in helmets and reflective vests are completing the remaining construction work. "Once completed, the plant is expected to generate 4.4 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough for about 160,000 households," said Wang Xinjin, project manager with Power Construction Corporation of China, or PowerChina. The project is expected to cut carbon dioxide emissions by around 2.4 million tonnes each year, supporting the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in expanding its clean energy supply and advancing its low-carbon transition, Wang added. Spanning about 20 square km, the project is PowerChina's first large-scale solar power project in the kingdom. PowerChina's Huadong Engineering Corporation Limited is responsible for its engineering, procurement, and construction. Chinese-made photovoltaic installation robots have also been deployed at the site, bringing greater automation to module installation. From solar panels to intelligent construction equipment, China's renewable-energy advances are increasingly being applied in energy infrastructure projects across the Gulf region. The UAE has accelerated renewable energy development in recent years to diversify its energy mix and has committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Several solar and wind projects involving Chinese companies have begun operations, harnessing the country's abundant sunshine and wind resources to generate clean electricity. In the desert south of Dubai, phases four and five of the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park present different approaches to converting sunlight into electricity. The fourth phase, built by Shanghai Electric Group, combines 700 MW of concentrated solar power with 250 MW of photovoltaic capacity. Its thermal storage system stores some collected solar energy for use after sunset. The project is expected to cut carbon emissions by about 1.6 million tonnes annually. Shanghai Electric also participated in the fifth phase, a 900-MW photovoltaic project now in operation, expected to reduce carbon emissions by about 1.18 million tonnes per year. Together, the two projects can cut emissions by about 2.78 million tonnes annually. Chinese companies are also helping the UAE explore renewable energy sources beyond solar power. The UAE Wind Program, the country's first utility-scale wind power project, was completed by PowerChina in 2023, with wind farms spanning islands, mountainous terrain and semi-desert landscapes. The project can serve more than 23,000 households each year and cut carbon emissions by around 120,000 tonnes annually. Meanwhile, as renewable energy capacity expands, ensuring a reliable power supply has become a major challenge, prompting China-UAE cooperation to move beyond stand-alone solar projects to integrated photovoltaic and large-scale energy storage projects. In Abu Dhabi, PowerChina is in the construction of a major solar and battery storage project designed to provide clean electricity around the clock. The northern section undertaken by the Chinese side includes 2.1 GW of direct-current photovoltaic capacity and a 7.75-gigawatt-hour battery energy storage system, designed to provide clean electricity around the clock and cut emissions by about 5.7 million tonnes annually once operational. Francesco La Camera, director-general of the International Renewable Energy Agency, said in a recent interview with Xinhua that China has made important contributions to the global energy transition by advancing technology and lowering the cost of clean energy equipment, making clean energy more affordable and accessible. Stronger cooperation in technology, financing and infrastructure could enable more countries to benefit from falling renewable energy costs and accelerate global emissions reduction, he said.
